utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday you indicated that you were aware of the takeover in 25 Prijedor and you were also asked about the outbreak of the 26 conflict in Kozarac. I believe you indicated that the alleged 27 killing of a soldier who was in a JNA uniform in Jakupovici was 28 one of the direct causes which led to disagreement between the 1 Serbs and Muslims. This disagreement between the Serbs and the 2 Muslims that was caused or triggered by the incident with the 3 soldier, this was the attack on Kozarac, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the -- well, that was about a month and a half later, 5 after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that something was 6 in the air, something was wrong. The situation was tense, there 7 was uncertainty, and we who were, who knew the situation a 8 little bit better, who followed the events, we knew that 9 something will act as a spark, and that spark was the killing of 10 that soldier. That was on the way to Kozarac at some kind of 11 division line between the Serbian and Muslim, Muslim 12 communities. That was between Banja Luka and Prijedor, 13 Jakupovici. That, as far as I know, was, in fact, one event that 15 triggered the attack - the conflicts between the Serbs and the 16 Muslims. Who attacked whom, whether Muslims attacked the Serbs, 17 Serbs the Muslims, I honestly do not know because I was not 18 there at that time and I could not -- this was not part of my 19 job. I was not that much interested. What I was mainly 20 concerned with was actually simply doing my work and I felt a 21 bit under pressure as a person living in the area. In my view, this was just one sparkle, but the whole 23 thing was hanging in the air and, in fact, it does not matter 24 who started and who killed whom, this was just one case because 25 living in Prijedor we learned that the situation became more and 26 more tense, that the tank was attacked, that a soldier was 27 killed, a local boy. Now, that was what happened. But that was 28 not the day that Kozarac was attacked. Kozarac was attacked, Kozarac was actually attacked two days later on Friday, that was on Friday. Then we had Saturday and actually on Sunday the fighting between Muslims and Serbs broke out between Kozarac and Omarska in that part of the line, along the line dividing the Muslim and Serbian villages. Was that clear enough? 6 Q. By the time you were working in the area as part of the commission, the area of Kozarac had been, essentially, entirely cleansed of the Muslim community, correct? 9 A. Not quite, not quite at that time. There was still some Muslims but not in Kozarac itself but, rather, in some villages towards Trnopolje. That was according to my information and according to my knowledge from the field. This was not 100 per cent cleansed. The cadastral municipality of Kozarac was not fully cleansed at that time. We are talking now about in September, October, November, there were still some Muslim people living in the cadastral municipality of Kozarac because Kozarac, as a cadastral municipality, is much larger, while the town itself of Kozarac had no Muslims left in Kozarac itself. 19 Q. You have explained to us much of the structure and work of the agricultural station. How many people worked for you as director of the agricultural service? How many people were you responsible for? 23 A. I was responsible for 12 people altogether. At the moment I have seven people only because our scope of activities was somewhat reduced during the wartime, but also I have people who work seasonally because we have our own production, we have the experimental farm. So, in fact, we need to take more workers when the season is in full swing. This is now an intermunicipal 1 service. We have more engineers, Masters of science and so on. 2 But the station never had more than 12 to 13 people permanently 3 employed. It never had more. At the moment we have only 4 seven. I was responsible for -- the largest number that I was 5 responsible for was 12 people during my rule, if I may put it 6 this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understood that you were, from what you testified yesterday, 8 extremely busy even before your appointment as director. I 9 presume those responsibilities and duties only increased after 10 your appointment as director?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say, I do work a great deal and I work hard. At 12 the same time, I am also a professional collaborator. I am a 13 court expert. I have my own farm also. So I was working on 14 several fronts and never had much time. When, of course, 15 I became the director, that was just another obligation, and in 16 the state of war it was all the more difficult, so that when 17 I had to leave in the morning, I had to do many of the things in 18 my office, my regular routine work, and then I left for the 19 field. I was not very enthusiastic about being on that 21 commission, but that was a necessity. There was nobody else to 22 do that. Also, I had been living in this part. I knew all the 23 villages and I knew Muslims, Croats and Serbs in the area 24 between Kozarac and Grmec, and I knew how to approach them, how 25 to talk to them. I never had any difficulty contacting people 26 and establishing good relations with them to complete the kind 27 of work which I started to do. I had no prejudice and I was doing my best. 1 I approached everybody openly, frankly, working in my domain. 2 I never touched upon matters which do not concern me. I only 3 deal with professional matters and that was all. So that, as a 4 man, as a human being, I never tried to be superficial in my 5 approach to work. I invested all of my energies into my duties 6 and I could come to any farmer, to any house owner. I could 7 look him in the eye and do my job fairly and I never ha problems 8 with people -- at least not until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the essential task of the commission was to go through the 10 areas you spoke of and determine whether or not any of the homes 11 or habitations were still livable, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the principal task of the commission. That was our 13 assignment, to establish how many houses were still habitable so 14 as to accommodate, so as to house, the refugees; whether they 15 met conditions, that is, whether the water supply was all right, 16 electricity, whether these houses were furbished, if somebody 17 had already moved in, then to establish who had moved in, how 18 many members of the family. We had also cadastral data, who was 19 the owner, the area or plots of land, and those were our 20 principal tasks, or if a person had moved in, why had he done 21 so. I never went into who was supposed to get a particular 23 house. We were simply to go out, make a record, take stock of 24 this, write down the protocol, turn it over to the central 25 commission and that would be that. Of course, sign the 26 protocol, all three members of the commission, but that was 27 that. As I have said, we issued no decisions, no ordinances nor 28 thing. We never issued any decisions, I mean, valid decisions that somebody would be entitled to use a particular house for half a year or for a year or something. Ours was simply to go out into the field, take stock of the situation, make a record of this and then submit it to the central commission. That was our principal assignment. 6 Q. You were part, therefore, of this process of going to private residences and determining whether they were habitable and then providing that information to the authorities of Republika Srpska so that it could be proclaimed as State property? 10 A. I did not really get your question. I did not understand well your question. 12 Q. Sure. The farms and homes which you surveyed were privately owned, correct? 14 A. Yes, privately owned, yes. Yes. They were all private property. 16 Q. OK. Those were homes in the area of Kozarac, Kamicani, Kozarusa? 18 A. Yes, there were houses in that area, and they -- those were Muslims mostly. They were mostly Muslim houses, that is, houses abandoned by their Muslim owners and they were treated as abandoned, as vacated houses but with private owners. 22 Q. Many of the homes in that area were no longer habitable. They had been destroyed during the conflict, correct? 24 A. There were some which were destroyed and some of them were looted. Of course, in combat operations quite a number of them were destroyed, shall we say, about 40 per cent were not habitable, which did not meet criteria, either because they had been destroyed or looted, plundered or set fire to. But sometimes owners (and there were such instances), when the owner was leaving the house who thought he had to leave the house, he would put it on fire himself, so that there is no some general law, I mean, applicable to all situations and say, "This was so and so and so and so". No, there were all sorts of things and sometimes owners simply torched their own houses themselves. I mean, if his mind was set to go, then rather than leave it to somebody else, he would simply put it on fire. There were such cases. But it was 60 per cent of the houses were habitable, of those houses which we surveyed and during my time on the commission. 12 Q. Did you happen to be on the main street of Kozarac during the time you were conducting your work? 14 A. Did I happen -- what? 15 Q. Were you in central Kozarac and on the main street, Marsala Tita, at some point? 17 A. Well, I used to pass those streets. That was the High Street in Kozarac. 19 Q. Did you notice that Dusko Tadic's home had written on it, "Serbian house, do not touch"? 21 A. There was such an inscription, yes, "Serb house, do not touch" on some houses, but there were no people in them. We went into those houses. We did survey them. There would be no one in them, but they did have this graffiti, "Serb house, do not touch", and we would go in and then make a record of what was there and turn it over to the municipal commission. I mean, a person or the owner might have written that and left, and some people also appropriated the right and appropriated two or three 1 houses, that is, misappropriated the right and appropriated two 2 or three houses prior to this commission, because there was a 3 general disarray. There were no authorities, no real power. It 4 was wartime so that it was -- so that some people simply tried 5 to profit from the situation. You know what I mean? When an atomic bomb drops and 7 it is a mess all over. It is very difficult really for one to 8 decide what is the wisest thing to do, and it is very easy to 9 have -- to be clever, to be wise after the event. We were 10 simply caught there unawares. Complete and overall chaos 11 reigned there and even people who were known to be very poised 12 persons panicked at the time because we -- nobody, nobody 13 thought that after 50 years of normal life we would again come 14 to experience this. There were very few people remembering that vast, long 16 time ago. Most of us lived normally; only those who were 17 preparing all this and preparing the ground for all this knew 18 about this. All the rest of us were shocked by it. It was a 19 very difficult moment for us. It was very difficult to decide 20 what to do, while women, children, what to do with them. Some 21 people said one thing, other people said some other thing. It 22 was really difficult to know what was the best to do or what was 23 one supposed to do, how to go about all these things. Some people may say that they did know what would 25 happen, but I did not know. Had I known it, I would have slept 26 well, but as it was, I did not know about this so that I was 27 really caught unawares and very many -- and there were too many 28 things in all, too many things vague, too many moot points, moot questions, something that one could not read even -- find in books and for normal people it was a shock. I really could not wish it on anybody. 4 Q. At the time you were examining these private homes and determining which were habitable, they were still privately owned and still the property of their rightful owners? Once you determined that a home was habitable, you provided that information to the authorities of Republika Srpska, is that correct? 10 A. Yes, these were houses which the municipality took for temporary use. It proclaimed them its property, and it was allocated to people not for ever, but only for use for three, six or 12 months -- at least at the time when I was part of the process. We would go out, make a, take stock of the situation, then turn over, turn over this to the commission and then they granted leases or permits for three, six or 12 months, but nobody got such houses for permanent use. I mean, nobody could come and say: "I have left another municipality and another house somewhere, so I am taking up this house". No, no permanent ownership rights. You could get a house for use for three, six or 12 months and you had to sign the protocol saying that you have taken up this house and when you were going out again. 24 Q. Do you know how much compensation was provided to the Muslim owners when their property was appropriated by Republika Srpska? 26 A. No compensation was paid, as far as I know, neither in cash nor in property, nor anything. 28 Q. You have indicated that at the time there were people who needed residences; there were more people who needed residences than there were residences available. Was there a priority system developed for who would receive those homes, flats or apartments which were available? 5 A. This is something that was not within my province. This is the central commission of the municipality which they did. They had some criteria. They had a set of priorities on the basis of which they ruled. I really do not know what they were. 9 Q. But you are ---- 10 A. I guess the number of children, how many members in a family. I would not really know, but it would be my guess that that was one of the conditions, one of the priorities, I would say. Although, of course, sometimes, as we are want to do, sometimes we give to somebody who is least needy and those who are more in need are not given something. Those are those who go outside priorities, but otherwise ---- 17 Q. You were aware that service during the war, during the conflict, was one of the priorities or one of the factors that gave a person a priority? 20 A. Well, it is rather likely, yes, I guess they would have some priority there. There must have been instances of that kind, or a child who is closer to his mother, of course, will be breast fed before the child who is further away from his mother. So I think that some were given the houses even though they were not really entitled to on the basis of some other priorities. Some may have been given a bigger house or given a house sooner simply because they were closer to authorities. I mean, these things do happen. 1 Q. That is all I have. Thank you. 2 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 4 MR. WLADIMIROFF: Just one question, your Honour. 5 Q. I have just one question. Mr. Dasic, you told us yesterday that your commission covered the area of the cadastral municipality of Kozarac. You explained that your commission WAS working in Kozarac, a part of Trnopolje called Hrnici, Kozarusa, Kamicani and a part of Dera and a part of Bozici, is that right? 10 A. Yes, it is. That was the area covered by my commission, except that we did not finish all the work because the weather changed, the conditions became more difficult, and at 1st January the commission stopped working and I stopped heading the commission. 14 Q. I understand that. Was Dusko Tadic visiting Trnopolje camp with you whilst you were working with him on the commission? 16 A. At that time Dusko Tadic was not in the Trnopolje camp. He was on the commission with me. 18 MR. WLADIMIROFF: Thank you. That is all I ask, your Honour. 19 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger? 20 MR. TIEGER: May I have a moment, your Honour? No, nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 23 JUDGE STEPHEN: Witness, were there any records kept of the time, the times, rather, I suppose, each day when you were engaged on work of the commission, written records? 26 A. There is a written record at the Prijedor municipality, except that I did not have the possibility -- I did not see that decision. There is an official decision saying that I am the head of the commission, what am I supposed to do, what is my assignment and things like that. 3 Q. No, I do not mean that, but were there daily records kept of the hours when you and your two other members of the commission were out in the field doing the work you have described? 6 A. Officially, no, but I kept my own record book, that is, I had my log book and then I noted that down, but had somebody -- did somebody else have such a record, no. It was simply a question of trust; that the commission would pick out the time which was most suitable. Whether we would work for three hours or for five hours or 10 hours, it depended on various things. It could depend on the head of the commission. In this particular case, it depended on me really, whether I would go out at 7 o'clock in the morning and stay until there was daylight. It really depended on a number of objective and subjective things and on the men who headed the commission, at least that is the tradition in that area, that a man who is put in charge of something is really responsible and he decides about these things, whether we would stay out for longer, for longer hours or whether we would work shorter hours but harder. It really depended on whether a car was available, on my free time, on weather conditions and so on and so forth. Sometimes we went out later and returned later, sometimes we went out earlier and so on. 25 Q. What I am concerned with is whether you have still in your possession your log book, do you? 27 A. I have to look for it. I do have it. I do have it somewhere. When I was about to leave to come here, I tried to find it and 1 I did not. After all, it was 1992. I am really sorry but 2 I must have it somewhere. It was my personal diary. So that 3 I will have to continue looking for it and I will try to send it 4 to show you that we really went out into the field, at what time 5 we set out and at what time we returned, if there was something 6 specific which I noted down just for my own sake. I have been a field worker for ages and I always kept 8 a kind of diary, and I do not remember names of people, but I do 9 remember other things. I am not going to say that I am a good 10 agronomist, but I think I am fairly knowledgeable about that 11 particular area of work.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The next question I wanted to ask you was, do you know whether 13 there would have been a record kept somewhere of the use of this 14 car when it was driven by the driver? Would he keep a record 15 and would that be maintained in some central office in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professional municipal drivers, they must have their travel 17 order and they must, of course, note down when they set out into 18 the field, when they returned and, of course, their fuel 19 consumption. I do not have this, but these records can be 20 traced because the drivers, they of course have to do that 21 because they are official cars, official vehicles or, rather, 22 municipal, so they have to put it down, the time they leave, the 23 time of departure, the time of return and things of that, the 24 fuel and everything else, except that we since if we used 25 private cars, then of course we did not do that or we did it for 26 our own sake. But when I used the official vehicle of the 27 agricultural station, then of course I needed a travel order 28 always, time of departure, time of return, fuel consumption and everything else. You had to put it down to justify your costs and all these things. 3 Q. Those records would still be maintained somewhere in the opstina I suppose, would they? 5 A. Yes, oh, yes, one would be able to trace them. It must be in existence somewhere because it is not -- it was not so long ago, and so these documents are kept for 10 years at least under our old laws. I do not know how it is now. 9 Q. The next question on a quite different topic: when Mr. Tadic accompanied you, as a member of the commission, on these journeys, what was he wearing? Was he wearing a uniform or was he wearing ordinary civilian clothes? 13 A. Mr. Tadic did not ask for me to be appointed to the commission. The commission was appointed by the Executive Board of the municipality ---- 16 Q. No. 17 A. --- of the Municipal Assembly. 18 Q. No, you misunderstand my question. I am simply asking, when he did accompany you what clothes did he wear? Did he wear a uniform or did he wear civilian clothes? 21 A. We all wore or, rather, tried to wear uniforms because it was safer for field work. I was also in a uniform. It was also fashionable in a way, whoever could lay his hands on a uniform. I mean, he felt and was more privileged, but I know that my uniform was poorer and Tadic's was better. But, in any event, I was not particularly keen on uniform, but I still wanted to have it because the situation was really not under control. It was easier to approach people or talk to people. When you would be in civilian clothes, then it could appear as if you were looking for something again privately for your own sake and, therefore, it was better. So I tried to combine things. I could not really lay my hands on a whole uniform, but I tried to combine. I did not have footwear which belonged to it, but our geodesic, she did not have uniform, she had civilian clothes, and Tadic and I were in uniforms and it was really advisable. 9 Q. Do you remember what sort of uniform Mr. Tadic wore? We have heard of camouflage uniforms, we have heard of SMB uniforms. Which was he wearing or did he wear different uniforms at different times, and police uniforms also we have heard of? 13 A. As far as I can remember, as far as I can remember, Mr. Tadic had a multi-coloured, what we called a camouflage uniform, not the SMB of the old Yugoslavia. Those were worn by ordinary soldiers, by simple soldiers, who had no money to buy something else, a camouflage uniform. But we tried to somehow come by those new uniforms to look slightly better, to look like civilised soldiers, or whichever way you care to put it, although it was difficult to be that. 21 JUDGE STEPHEN: Good. Thank you. 22 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Just a few questions. What colour was the camouflage uniform? Is it a multi-colour, brown, green, light brown, dark brown, coffee colour? 25 A. You know, I am slightly handicapped. I really do not recall colours when they are not in front of my eyes. I know it was many colours, whichever colours were worn at the time. I really could not -- I am simply unable to describe what colour a person 1 was wearing at a particular time. I never can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That is OK. If homes were taken from individuals in Kozarac, 3 taken from them, prior to October 1st 1992, I gather your 4 commission would not have been involved in that because the 5 commission did not exist, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tadic told me (and I was also aware of the fact) that 7 there had been two commissions before me whose assignment was 8 also to survey all this property which we then started doing, 9 but of course they failed. When our commission was established, 10 we knew that we would succeed because the three men appointed to 11 it were all very serious, very thorough and we would really do 12 good work, and Mr. Tadic when we met, because he also did not 13 know me really, he said: "I will congratulate you if you 14 succeed" and I told him: "Just you listen what this seasoned 15 man will tell you and we shall succeed certainly", because one 16 has to know how to work in a village. You have to know how to 17 approach a villager, and if you have shown him that you are 18 honest, that you are decent, then you cannot fail, and there is 19 no distinction between rich and poor. You have to know how to approach it, and I have been 21 working with villagers for years. So I knew how to approach a 22 man, how to talk to people, how serious, what kind of a 23 language, when to accept a cup of coffee from him or when not to 24 accept it and that was my personal experience. For instance, 25 I never allowed the commission to accept a cup of coffee in a 26 house because then it would meaning sitting down and that would 27 be that. So I never allowed such -- these kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know what commissions Mr. Tadic was talking about, the 1 two commissions that existed before October 1st, for the 2 reassignment or whatever of houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were similar to ours, except that they had no agronomists 4 on these commissions. They were commissions which were composed 5 of inexperienced people, mostly young, some girls who were 6 either lawyers or, for instance, geodesics, surveyors. But they 7 simply were not up to the task. I never really went into it. 8 I did not want to. I did not particularly care to learn who 9 were people were on these commissions. But, as far as I know, 10 they were all rather inexperienced and that is why they did not 11 succeed in completing the business.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. Tadic was assigned to this commission? You 13 have testified about your long and good experience. Was the 14 other member of the commission a woman, but a woman who had this 15 agronomist experience? If not agronomist, it was -- what was 16 the experience of the other member of the commission, the 17 woman? She was not a lawyer, I gather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was, no, she was not a lawyer. She was not a lawyer. She 19 was a land surveyor. She carried those cadastral instruments 20 and worked for the cadastral office, for the cadastre. She 21 could identify every house. She knew owners because she had 22 those cadastre books. She was a very serious professional. She 23 knew how to take, where to take us. She knew where everything 24 was and that is this field experience which is of tremendous 25 importance when you go out into the field. When you have a 26 dilettante who does not know anything, who does not know whose 27 house is where, what is the cadastral municipality -- the 28 cadastral area or the books or who is the owner of a particular house, and she had that kind of experience. She knew that. This little Gordana Sobot whom we called "Goca". She has been with the cadastre office for some 20 years. 4 Q. Do you know whether Mr. Tadic had any prior experience in this type of work? 6 A. I could not tell you that, but at that time since it was being done at the Local Commune where Mr. Tadic was in a way the head of that Local Commune, that is, I think, how he came to be appointed to the commission because it was his Local Commune. Whether he had any kind of experience in this kind of work, I really could not tell you. He was a third member of the commission, and the two of us were the main members. We were the ones who conducted the whole business, but it was simply to have a local person because we were working in that area so we needed a person from that area to be with us. 16 Q. Can you make an estimate as to how many homes you handled, that is, how many homes were transferred, if I may use that expression? I just do not know what other expression to use, but how many homes were given to families or individuals by the Republika Srspka by your commission? 21 A. At that time while we still worked, over 90 houses had already been surveyed and were being moved -- and some of them were being moved in, because as we went over them and we were -- at my initiative, we would start one day from one end and the next day from the other, because there were people who were trying to misappropriate these things. There were some tractors transporting furniture. There were all sorts of things. I mean, the people really thought that they could take away 1 things that were not theirs because the situation was so 2 chaotic. So we thought -- I thought it would be better if we 4 always started from a different part of the area, from either 5 [redacted] or Kozarac or something. But I think that about 90 6 per cent were by that time issued these decisions and could move 7 in and for others the decisions were pending. I know that many 8 people were satisfied with the work of the commission because we 9 had done a good job of work in some 10 or 15 days already. So 10 that protocols were made and so that decisions were beginning to 11 be issued, and what they would be given for use, what they had 12 to look after, because if they were to move out of that 13 particular house after three or six months, they also had to 14 have an inspection to see whether the house was as it was when 15 they had moved in. I believe that had we had another month at 16 our disposable that the situation would have been quite clear 17 but, unfortunately, the weather conditions were such that we had 18 to interrupt. But, as far as I can remember, it was more than 150 20 houses that we surveyed during that time. As I said, I cannot 21 find the diary, that log book, that I had there. I had the 22 exact number. Whether it was 170 or 155, I do not know, but it 23 must have been over 150 homes. Over 90, as we were going on 24 with our work, 90 of those were already being moved in, that is, 25 decisions had been issued for them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you surveyed 150, approximately, and of the 150, 90 had 27 already been surveyed and approved as being subject to 28 occupation? 1 A. About 90, yes, about 90, yes, had already been distributed. 2 Q. So am I correct then that it was 60, approximately, houses that you surveyed and of that number you determined, well, you surveyed 150 but 90 of them had already been surveyed, but you did beginning work on the remaining and then made a decision as to whether they were habitable and then subject to being assigned to someone, is that correct? Is that the number? 8 A. I hope you understand me about the 150 houses we surveyed, and some of these 150 had been settled on the basis of our own protocols, of the protocols issued by my commission. So between 90 and 150, some 60 houses had no documents yet. Later, these were also given special approvals for settlement for some people. But when that was done, how it was done, to whom it was given, I do not know. After 1st January 1993, I had nothing to do with any of such commissions so I cannot tell you what happened later and I was too busy at that time. 17 Q. Who made the decision then to make the actual assignment after you made a determination of suitability? 19 A. There was a central commission of the cadastral property service and they were the ones who were entitled, who were authorised, who had the criteria, as to the distribution and allocation of these houses. This was not part of our brief. Whatever we did would be nothing. It would be not legally valid. We could only provide protocols of the suitability and habitability, but they decided whether this, that or the other person would be given that house because they were empowered to do that by the Assembly of the municipality of Prijedor. They had a special rubber stamp and that was the central commission for the whole of the municipality; so to get that was a legal document really. 2 Q. So that was the group you testified about yesterday, they made the final decision, is that correct? I think you testified yesterday that it was. 5 A. Yes, right, right. 6 Q. What was the name of that organisation, do you know, or the authorities? 8 A. That was the cadastral property ownership service for the municipality of Prijedor. 10 Q. You then would not know who was actually given the houses that you surveyed? 12 A. In my area, some 90 per cent of the houses were given to refugees from Cazin, Krupa, from Bihac, Bugojno, Travnik, mostly refugees, because when I was thinking professionally this was good land, good for intensive farming and these people, in fact, needed my help, professional help, because they came from higher altitudes, used to different kinds of farming. So they would have to learn to farm in this new area with new kinds of products, produce, and in fact that is how I viewed the whole situation. That is why I professionally and privately was interested in who was getting this, not the names, but all kinds of people were settling there. In 90 per cent of those new settlers came from these places that I mentioned. Many of them are still there now and they do have a problem to adjust to new technology, to a new climate, to new sort of soil, because they were used to be working and living at altitudes of 1500 metres, while we are now talking about the altitude of 200 metres. So there are different varieties, different kinds of plants grow there, and this is my own observation now that these people need a lot of help. 4 Q. Do you know how many of those people were Muslims? 5 A. You mean those who settled, who are settled there? 6 Q. Yes. 7 A. Those who were given these houses, the use of the houses? I know that there are many mixed marriages, but not Muslims as such, those who have been coming from Cazin, but I know there were some members who were Muslim perhaps in mixed marriages. Maybe a husband was a Muslim or the wife was -- the wife Serb and so on. There were some mixed marriages. Two cases, I know, two Muslims had Serbian wives, for instance. They themselves served in the army of Republika Srpska and so they came to live there. These are the two cases I know, but there are many other mixed marriages, people coming from the regions that I described earlier and settled here in Kozarac -- in and around Kozarac. 18 Q. One final question: you testified you felt that Mr. Tadic had every reason to have extremist views. What did you mean by that? Well, since following the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, within a month and a half following that recognition, the times were very difficult, very hard. There was a lot of intolerance, hatred, something that one can hardly imagine could happen. I do not know what their behaviour was like, and what happened during the clashes in and around Kozarac. I thought that he must have felt the tension. Although I know that people in Kozarac lived together in peace and quiet, I would be coming earlier to Kozarac, to Omarska and so on, and I would be eating, drinking with them, socialising with them and they were living together. But within a month and a half after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it became quite tense. People were insulting each other. There were many abnormal forms of behaviour, insulting each other, as I said earlier. You could not even go into a pub or a cafe because you never knew who would tell you what and say to you what. So that is what I had in mind. 11 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Thank you. Mr. Wladimiroff? 12 MR. WLADIMIROFF: Nothing arises, your Honour, thank you. 13 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger? 14 MR. utterances.text: 6 Q. We have referred to military service as well as work obligation. Were they two different things during this period in 1992? 9 A.
